{{DesktopLinux}}

Common OpenSSH client ops: log into a remote machine, run one-off commands, copy files, and tunnel ports over an encrypted channel. Everything here is typed on your local Linux machine; the remote side only needs a running <code>sshd</code>.

New to SSH? Every command has a built-in manual — try <code>man ssh</code>, <code>man ssh_config</code> or [https://tldr.sh tldr ssh] for short examples.

== Set up key login ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
ssh user@host                            # first connection: type the password, or for most cloud providers, via the web console shell
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "user@laptop"   # create ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and its .pub
ssh-copy-id user@host                    # install the public half on the server
ssh user@host                            # no password from now on
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
user: your username on the remote machine
host: IP address or URL of the remote machine
</blockquote>

The private key never leaves your machine; the server only needs to stores the public key, one key per line, in <code>~/.ssh/authorized_keys</code>.

== Connecting ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
ssh user@host                         # log in as user on host
ssh -p 2222 user@host                 # non-standard port
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my_key user@host        # use my_key as private key
ssh user@host command                 # run one command instead of spawning a shell
ssh user@host -N                      # no remote command: forward ports only
ssh user@host 'command 1; command 2'  # several commands: quote and separate commands by ;
ssh -t user@host tmux attach          # -t: force a TTY, for interactive programs. Opposite is -T
ssh -J user1@proxy:2222 user2@host    # -J*: proxy jump, connects to host as user2, via the intermediate (proxy) machine on port 2222
ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new user@host # accept an unknown host key once
ssh -G host                           # print effective configurations for a given host
ssh -v user@host                      # debug the connection; -vv and -vvv go further
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
*: This may be useful when you need to connect to a remote DB, etc. behind a firewall that is only accessible via machines on the local network. You first connect to a proxy machine on that network which accepts ssh from other networks, then ssh to the final destination via the proxy.
</blockquote>

== Keys ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
ssh-keygen -t ed25519                        # new key in ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (+ .pub)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_work -C "deploy@laptop"   # a named key, with a comment
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096                    # use RSA instead of ed25519 for legacy compatibility
ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519           # change the passphrase
ssh-keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519           # print the public half of a private key
ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub       # fingerprint of a key
ssh-keygen -R host                           # forget a host's key in known_hosts
ssh-copy-id user@host                        # install the default key on a server
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_work.pub user@host  # install one specific key
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''<code>ssh</code> enforces key permissions:''' It will not accept a private key where any other user has read permission. Keep <code>~/.ssh</code> at <code>700</code> and private keys at <code>600</code> (<code>chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519</code>). 
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
Good security practice: Always protect your private keys with a passphrase.
</blockquote>

== ~/.ssh/config ==

For frequently accessed machines, set up a connection profile in `~/.ssh/config` on your local machine. 

<syntaxhighlight lang="text" copy>
Host mySSHRemote 
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    Port 2222
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_work

Host *.internal.example.com
    ProxyJump mySSHRemote

Host myLegacyRemote
    HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa          # for old servers
    PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms +ssh-rsa

Host *                         # global defaults: keep this block LAST
    ServerAliveInterval 30     # ping every 30 s, so idle NAT and firewall sessions survive
    ServerAliveCountMax 3
    AddKeysToAgent yes         # load a key into the agent on first use
    ControlMaster auto         # reuse one TCP connection for every later session to the 
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p # save the TCP connections to the specified path, with automatic naming. %r: remote user, %h: host name %p: port
    ControlPersist 10m         # cache TCP connection for 10 min after disconnection
</syntaxhighlight>

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
mkdir -p ~/.ssh/cm              # ControlPath does not create the directory
ssh -F ~/.ssh/otherconf host    # use an alternative config file
ssh -O check host               # is a shared connection open?
ssh -O exit host                # close shared connection, and every session using it
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''For each option, the first value found wins.'''  Hence the catch-all <code>Host *</code> should always be at the bottom.
</blockquote>

== Encrypted ssh keys: <code>ssh-agent</code> ==

If you use encrypted ssh keys, <code>ssh-agent</code> allow you to cache those keys unencrypted in RAM over one login session on local machine, so you do not have to provide the passphrase on each use.

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"            # start an agent in this shell
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519         # load a key. If key encryped, asks for the passphrase once
ssh-add -t 8h ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # -t: automatically drop the key after 8 hours
ssh-add -l                        # print fingerprints of the loaded keys
ssh-add -L                        # print full public keys of the loaded keys
ssh-add -d ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      # remove one key
ssh-add -D                        # remove every key
ssh-agent -k                      # kill this agent
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
 <code>AddKeysToAgent yes</code> in <code>~/.ssh/config</code> loads keys into the agent on first use.
</blockquote>

== Copying files ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
scp file1.txt user@host:/tmp/          # upload
scp -P 2222 file1.txt user@host:/tmp/  # note: scp's port flag is -P, NOT -p
scp user@host:~/file1.txt /tmp/        # download a file
scp 'user@host:/var/log/*.log' .       # download multiple files matching the glob: remember to quote remote path when * is used
scp -r dir/ user@host:~/folder1        # download a whole directory
rsync -avz --progress dir/ user@host:/tmp/   # sync changes
sftp user@host                         # interactive: ls, get, put, bye
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
Note <code>rsync</code> must be installed both on your local machine and the remote server to work.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
Prefer <code>rsync</code> for large or repeated transfers, as it transfers only the differences and can resume when transfer is interrupted.
</blockquote>

== Port forwarding ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host        # local 8080 forwards to host port 80
ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@host    # local 5432 forwards to host, which then forwards to db.internal 5432 (proxy connect)
ssh -R 9000:localhost:3000 user@host      # reverse forward: the server's 9000 forwards to your local 3000
ssh -D 1080 user@host                     # make host accessible as a SOCKS5 proxy on localhost:1080
ssh -N -f -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host  # background tunnel only, no interactive shell
ssh -O exit user@host                     # close the backgrounded tunnel
</syntaxhighlight>

The same forwardings in config, for a tunnel you start by name:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text" copy>
Host dbtunnel
    HostName db.example.com
    LocalForward 5432 localhost:5432   # -L 8080:localhost:80 by default for `ssh dbtunnel`
    SessionType none                   # background tunnel only
</syntaxhighlight>

== Escape sequences ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Escape !! Action
|-
| <code>~.</code> || disconnect
|-
| <code>~^Z</code> || suspend ssh, back to the local shell
|-
| <code>~#</code> || list the forwarded connections
|-
| <code>~C</code> || open ssh command line: add <code>-L</code>, <code>-R</code> or <code>-D</code> to the live session
|-
| <code>~?</code> || list all escapes
|}

<blockquote>
Inside an interactive session, escape sequences are recognised only at the start of a line.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
<code>~C</code> is disabled by default. To enable, add to `~/.ssh/config`:

<syntaxhighlight lang="text" copy>
Host *
  EnableEscapeCommandline yes
</syntaxhighlight>
</blockquote>

== Troubleshooting ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Symptom !! Fix
|-
| <code>Permission denied (publickey)</code> || Incorrect key or key-host/user mismatch: run <code>ssh -vvv user@host</code> for more details
|-
| <code>Too many authentication failures</code> || the agent offers more keys than the server allows attempts: add <code>IdentitiesOnly yes</code> to that host's block to only use keys explicitely configured for that host
|-
| <code>REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!</code> || the server's key changed: this could either be a server-side reset or a man-in-the-middle attack: confirm with the server's admin whether a legitimate reset took place before running <code>ssh-keygen -R host:port</code> to accept the change
|-
| <code>Connection refused</code> || wrong port, <code>sshd</code> down, or a firewall: test with <code>nc -vz host 22</code>
|-
| <code>Connection timed out</code> || nothing answers at all: a firewall is dropping the packets, or the host is unreachable
|-
| the session freezes after some idle || consider adding <code>ServerAliveInterval 60</code> in the config file to keep the session alive by sending keep-alive signals every 60s
|}
